summary: Specifies the steps an IPv6 host takes to automatically configure its interfaces. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 2462.

eli5.summary: A computer can work out its own address when it joins a network, like a new student finding their own desk.

questions: what is ipv6 stateless address autoconfiguration
how do ipv6 hosts get addresses without a server
subtitle: How IPv6 hosts automatically configure their own addresses without a server.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts need to obtain working addresses and connect to networks without manual configuration or dedicated servers, but also without creating chaos where two hosts accidentally use the same address.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts combine a well-known link-local prefix with a unique interface token to create their own link-local address, then verify its uniqueness before using it. For site-local and global addresses, routers advertise prefixes that hosts combine with their interface token. Duplicate Address Detection ensures no two hosts use the same address.
tldr.outcome: Stateless address autoconfiguration enables plug-and-play IPv6 networking. Small networks can work without any servers or manual setup. This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 2462, and the standard has since evolved further.

today: RFC 1971 was obsoleted by RFC 2462, which has since been superseded by RFC 4862. However, the core principles of stateless address autoconfiguration remain unchanged in modern IPv6. Stateless autoconfiguration is widely deployed and is a key enabler of IPv6's plug-and-play networking capabilities. It complements stateful autoconfiguration mechanisms like DHCPv6, allowing administrators to choose the right approach for their network.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPv6 defines two address autoconfiguration approaches: stateless and stateful. This RFC specifies the stateless mechanism, which requires minimal configuration of routers and no dedicated servers, allowing hosts to generate and configure their own addresses.

The process combines two pieces of information: a network prefix (advertised by routers) and an interface token (derived locally, often from the interface's link-layer address). The result is a unique IPv6 address. Three address types can be autoconfigured: link-local (for local-link communication), site-local (for site scope), and global (for worldwide routing).
sections.eli5: Stateless autoconfiguration means each computer figures out its own address using just two things: a name prefix the network tells it, and a unique identifier that's already built into its network card. No server needed.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The specification was designed around five core goals. First, manual configuration of individual machines should not be required before connecting them to a network. Second, small sites with a single link should not need a server or router to enable communication between nodes; link-local addresses alone should suffice. Third, large multi-site organizations should not require a stateful server to configure site-local or global addresses.

Fourth, address configuration should facilitate site renumbering when networks change providers. This is achieved through address leasing, where addresses have preferred and valid lifetimes, allowing graceful transitions between old and new prefixes. Fifth, administrators must be able to specify which autoconfiguration mechanisms (stateless, stateful, or both) are in use. Routers advertise this via flags in Router Advertisement messages.
sections.eli5: The five design goals are: computers should figure it out automatically, small networks should work without servers, big networks shouldn't need servers either, networks should be able to renumber gracefully, and administrators should be able to choose what kind of autoconfiguration happens.

sections.title: Creating Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
The first step in autoconfiguration happens whenever an interface becomes enabled: the host creates a link-local address. A link-local address combines the well-known link-local prefix FE80::/10 with an interface token. The interface token must be at least somewhat unique on the link; if it exceeds 118 bits, autoconfiguration fails.

Before assigning a link-local address to an interface, the host must verify that the address is not already in use on the link through Duplicate Address Detection (DAD). This procedure sends Neighbor Solicitation messages targeting the tentative address. If another node is already using it, or if two nodes are simultaneously trying to use the same address, they will detect each other and one of them must stop. Link-local addresses, once successfully verified, have infinite valid and preferred lifetimes.
sections.eli5: A link-local address is like getting a temporary seat number in your local classroom. The prefix is 'FE80' (it never changes), and your number is based on your network card's address. But before you sit down, you check that nobody else is already sitting there.

sections.title: Duplicate Address Detection
sections.content:
Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) is performed on all unicast addresses before they are assigned to an interface. While each address could theoretically be tested individually, when stateless autoconfiguration is used, address uniqueness is determined solely by the interface token. Therefore, if the link-local address (which is the first address created from a token) is unique, all other addresses created from the same token will also be unique.

The procedure works by sending Neighbor Solicitation messages to a solicited-node multicast address, asking if any node is already using the tentative address. The interface joins the all-nodes multicast address and the solicited-node multicast address before sending solicitations, ensuring it can receive both responses and detect competing attempts. An address is deemed unique if no positive responses arrive within a timeout period (typically a few seconds) after sending the required number of solicitations. If a duplicate is detected, the address cannot be assigned, and manual configuration becomes necessary.
sections.eli5: Duplicate Address Detection is like raising your hand and calling out your address: 'Is anyone here named 2001:db8::1?' If someone says yes, you can't use that name. If nobody answers, it's yours.

sections.title: Creating Global and Site-Local Addresses
sections.content:
After establishing a link-local address, hosts wait for Router Advertisements or send Router Solicitations to discover what prefixes are available. Router Advertisements contain Prefix Information options that specify which network prefixes are associated with the link, along with flags indicating whether stateless autoconfiguration, stateful autoconfiguration, or both should be used.

For each advertised prefix marked with the Autonomous Address Configuration flag, the host appends its interface token to the prefix to form a new address. These addresses have preferred and valid lifetime values that the host must track. A preferred address can be used for new communication; a deprecated address should only be used for existing communications. When a valid lifetime expires, the address becomes invalid and must not be used. This mechanism enables graceful site renumbering: administrators can advertise new prefixes alongside old ones, giving applications time to migrate before old addresses become invalid.
sections.eli5: The router is like a teacher announcing: 'Our school is now in district 2001:db8::/32, and students should use stateless autoconfiguration to build their full addresses.' Each student takes that prefix and adds their own unique token to make a complete address.
